No. Amcor's gross margin did not improve through FY2023; it declined. Gross profit as a % of net sales was 21.2% in FY2021, 19.4% in FY2022 and 18.5% in FY2023 (gross profit $2,732M, $2,820M, $2,725M). Earlier years also trended down: 21.0% in FY2017, 19.9% in FY2018, 19.0% in FY2019. Gross margin is also of limited use as a metric for Amcor, because the percentage is distorted by the pass-through of raw material costs. Higher resin costs raise net sales dollars with roughly no added profit, which mechanically lowers the margin %. Amcor attributes the FY2023 decline mainly to this pass-through effect plus disposed operations (the Russian business). Excluding currency (-$78M) and disposed/ceased operations (-$73M), gross profit rose $56M on favorable operating cost performance, so underlying profit dollars were healthier than the margin % suggests. Adjusted EBIT margin tells a similar story: total 11.7% in FY2022 vs 10.9% in FY2023, with about 90 bps of the FY2023 level attributed to the pass-through of raw material costs and inflation. Better measures are gross profit dollars, adjusted EBIT dollars, or margin excluding pass-through.

Operating margin is not a useful metric for American Express. As a card issuer and payments network, AmEx does not report cost of sales or an operating income line the way an industrial company does (the 'operating margin' in the retrieved pages comes from AES, a utility, and is defined as revenue less cost of sales, so it is not relevant to AmEx). AmEx's results are driven by discount revenue, net card fees, net interest income and provisions for credit losses, and it is assessed on revenues net of interest expense, pretax income, net income, and credit metrics. On those measures, 2022 was mixed rather than clearly improving: revenues net of interest expense rose 25% (27% FX-adjusted), but net income fell to $7.5 billion ($9.85 per share) from $8.1 billion ($10.02 per share) in 2021, because of a $617 million credit reserve build versus a $2.5 billion reserve release in the prior year and net losses in the Amex Ventures portfolio versus significant gains the year before. So a margin-improvement conclusion cannot be drawn from the pages; profitability fell in 2022 even as revenue grew strongly.

The pages do not give Boeing's consolidated gross margin figures (revenue and cost of sales) for FY2022, so I cannot compute or confirm an improving gross margin trend from them. Gross margin is also a weak metric for Boeing, because program accounting spreads tooling, non-recurring and production costs over a program's accounting quantity and records reach-forward losses and abnormal production costs as lump-sum charges. Reported cost of sales, and so gross margin, therefore swings with estimate changes rather than underlying performance. As of Dec 31, 2022, the 767, 777X and 787 programs had near break-even or single-digit margins and the 777X had near break-even gross margins. Past charges include the $3.5B 787 loss in Q4 2021, the $6.5B 777X reach-forward loss in Q4 2020, and abnormal 787 production costs of $1.7B cumulative through 2022 with the estimate raised to $2.8B. The only 2022 positive noted is that the 100-unit increase in the 787 accounting quantity improved that program's margin. Overall, margins on the key programs remained very thin and the evidence does not show a clearly improving gross margin profile.

The pages provided do not include Verizon's FY2022 balance sheet (current assets such as receivables, inventories and prepaid expenses, and current liabilities), so a quick ratio cannot be computed from them. What they do show: cash and cash equivalents of only $2.6 billion at Dec 31, 2022, against $9.3 billion of debt, $5.6 billion of interest, $4.6 billion of operating lease payments, $9.4 billion of purchase obligations and $4.8 billion of C-Band commitments due within twelve months. A quick ratio based on cash plus receivables would therefore likely be well below 1.0 and would not by itself indicate strong liquidity. However, the ratio is of limited relevance for Verizon, a capital-intensive telecom with recurring subscription revenue. Its liquidity rests on operating cash flow ($37.1 billion in 2022) and access to external financing (commercial paper, credit facilities, debt issuance, asset-backed securitizations). Management states these sources are sufficient for the next 12 months and beyond. On that basis liquidity appears reasonable, but it is better judged by cash flow generation and financing access than by the quick ratio.

Yes, Verizon is capital intensive in FY 2022. Capital expenditures were $23.1 billion (including about $6.2 billion of C-Band spending) against revenues of $136.8 billion, roughly 17% of revenue (23,087/136,835 = 16.9%). Capex consumed about 62% of the $37.1 billion operating cash flow (23,087/37,141), cutting free cash flow to $14.1 billion. Verizon also says capex is necessary for ongoing operations and that it uses operating cash to fund network expansion and modernization.

No. Verizon's total debt was essentially flat to slightly lower: $150.6 billion at December 31, 2022 versus $150.9 billion at December 31, 2021, a decrease of about $0.3 billion. (The large increase was in 2021, when debt rose from $129.1 billion at end of 2020 to $150.9 billion.)

Walmart's unadjusted operating income margin rose by about 0.2 percentage points from FY2018 to FY2019. FY2019 operating income of $21,957M on total revenues of $514,405M is 4.27%, and FY2018 operating income of $20,437M on $500,343M is 4.08%, a change of +0.18 points, which rounds to +0.2. Using net sales instead gives 4.3% vs 4.1%, the same +0.2 points.
